The challenge here is how to estimate future memory growth for determining the admission threshold T T . To answer this, we first deep dive into the memory allocation behavior of Firecracker ( Agache et al., 2020 ) . We observe that the physical memory growth mainly comes from four sources: library loading, interpreter runtime caches, allocator operation, and CoW modifications to shared snapshot pages. A deep investigation shows that sandbox memory growth has a structured lifecycle rather than an arbitrary pattern. Library loading and interpreter caches dominate the cold-start phase and are largely determined by the sandbox template. Allocator operations and CoW modifications continue during running phase, but both shows slower marginal growth than the cold-start phase. The reason behind is that once allocators have expanded their arenas, subsequent allocations are often served from existing pages. Similarly, once shared pages have been privatized, later writes to the same pages no longer trigger additional CoW allocation. As a result, most sandboxes memory growth is typically bursty during cold start and much slower during running phase. Based on this observation, VenusRL uses two different predict heuristic for cold-start and running sandboxes. For cold-start phase sandboxes, VenusRL uses offline profiling of the same template to estimate memory growth, since sandboxes from the same template share the same runtime, dependencies, and initialization path. For running sandboxes, VenusRL estimates the recent growth rate from a short time window and uses this growth rate to estimate their short-term memory demand. At admission time, VenusRL accounts for both the recent growth of active sandboxes and the expected cold-start growth of the candidate one. It admits the candidate only after reserving sufficient headroom for this near-term growth, with a safety factor α \alpha to tolerate prediction bias. When sandbox memory usage is stable, VenusRL raises the threshold and admits more sandboxes; when memory is still growing quickly, VenusRL lowers the threshold and delays further admission. This mechanism allows VenusRL to increase deployment density while avoiding the unsafe behavior of admitting sandboxes solely based on current memory usage. Sandbox Migration. Although dynamic admission threshold substantially reduces OOM risk, it may still underestimate sudden memory bursts when sandbox footprints grow faster than the predictor. To improve robustness, VenusRL uses sandbox migration as a fallback mechanism. When the controller fails to allocate new physical pages for allocation request, VenusRL intercepts the resulting OOM exception signal before the failure propagates to the task. It then temporarily pauses all running sandboxes while preserving their in-memory states. It then selects the sandbox with the largest resident memory footprint and migrates only this sandbox to another resource worker. After migration, VenusRL recomputes the node’s memory usage and admission threshold. If the node still exceeds the safe threshold, VenusRL repeats the process. This incremental largest-first policy avoids unnecessary migration: VenusRL releases one sandbox’s memory at a time and stops as soon as the node returns to a safe state. To reduce migration overhead and limit its impact on the critical path, VenusRL uses the Mooncake transfer engine ( Qin et al., 2025b ) to transfer sandbox memory state directly between resource workers. This direct memory-state transfer avoids slow checkpoint-and-reload paths and allows VenusRL to quickly relieve memory pressure while preserving sandbox execution state. Upon migration, VenusRL resumes all paused running sandboxes. 5.2. Page Sharing RL algorithms such as PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) and GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) expand each prompt into a group of trajectories that, by construction, are launched from the same environment template. Within a group, sandboxes execute nearly identical setup code—loading the same dependencies, importing the same packages, materializing the same scratch files—so a large fraction of their pages remain byte-identical until divergent tool calls begin to write new state. VenusRL exploits this invariant to increase per-node sandbox density without weakening isolation. As shown in Figure 9 , VenusRL realizes intra-group sharing by decoupling three issues that the native fork/mmap path conflates, i.e., virtual-address ownership, physical-page residency, and write permission. Each sandbox keeps its own VMA (Virtual Memory Area) and page table, but read-only PTEs (Page Table Entry) from different sandboxes in a group may alias the same physical frame (shared residency), with write permission masked until a write actually occurs, i.e., lazy CoW. Two requirements must be satisfied. (i) Eager binding: sharing should be installed at sandbox creation, before any page fault, so that no sandbox ever allocates a redundant frame for a snapshot page (Figure 9 -left). (ii) Strict isolation: a write by one sandbox can’t be visible to its peers and compromised sandboxes can’t corrupt the shared backing store. VenusRL realizes this across two layers: a user-space group page pool and a kernel-side write-protected mapping. Figure 9 . Mechanism of Page Sharing. Group Page Pool At User Space. VenusRL maintains a per-group page pool indexed by guest-memory offset, using the environment template as the sharing key. Pages are populated lazily: when any sandbox in the group first accesses a page, VenusRL loads that page into the shared pool (Figure 9 -middle). For each memory offset, VenusRL allows only one sandbox to perform this first load at a time, so concurrent sandboxes always share the same populated page. Once populated, a pool entry is immutable: subsequent accesses from any group member find the frame already resident, with no per-sandbox allocation. Because the pool is keyed by template rather than by content hash, VenusRL never scans memory to discover sharing; every read-only snapshot page is shared by construction. Per-Sandbox Mapping And CoW At Kernel Level. Each sandbox maps its guest memory as a private, write-protected view over the page pool. Reads behave as ordinary guest-memory accesses, with the sandbox’s PTE silently aliasing a frame in the pool. A write is handled by allocating a private writable frame, copying the page contents, and rebinding only that sandbox’s PTE to the new frame. The pool entry and every other sandbox’s mapping are left untouched (Figure 9 -right). Because aliasing is performed at PTE granularity rather than by sharing whole memory regions, divergence is local—isolation is preserved at the same granularity that the sandbox boundary already enforces, and a compromised sandbox can corrupt only its own private frames. 6. Evaluation Figure 10 . Training performance of agentic RL systems under different batchsize and staleness. We implemented VenusRL with 24k lines of Python, Rust and Golang atop our internal team’s RL training framework, SGLang ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) , E2B ( E2B Development Team, 2024 ) and Firecracker ( Agache et al., 2020 ) . Our evaluation aims to answer the following questions: (1) How does VenusRL compare to state-of-the-art agentic RL systems in end-to-end training performance (§ 6.2 )? (2) How do the three core techniques in the priority-aware action scheduler contribute to performance (§ 6.3 )? (3) How effective is the environment resource manager in VenusRL (§ 6.4 )? 6.1. Experimental Setup Testbed. We conduct our experiments on a cluster of four servers, totaling 32 GPUs. Each node is equipped with eight NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, 180 Intel Xeon CPU cores, and 1.8 TB of host memory. Intra-node GPU communication utilizes 900 GB/s NVLink, while inter-node networking is handled by 400 Gb/s NVIDIA Mellanox InfiniBand. Specifically, we allocate 16 GPUs to generation and another 16 GPUs to training. Models and Workloads. We evaluate VenusRL using instruction-tuned Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-32B models ( Bai et al., 2023 ) , which provide strong tool-use and reasoning capabilities. We conduct experiments on representative SWE-agent tasks ( Yang et al., 2024b ) with the OpenSWE dataset ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , which contains 45,320 executable Docker environments spanning over 12.8K repositories, allowing agents to execute code, run test suites, and check formatting. For all agentic rollouts, we set the maximum output length to 128K tokens and limit each trajectory to at most 300 turns. We generate eight samples per prompt using the GRPO RL algorithm ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . We set the LLM generation temperature to 0.7 ( Yang et al., 2024a ) and configure the framework with a weight-version threshold of 2, discarding samples whose generation spans three or more weight versions. Baselines. We compare VenusRL against three state-of-the-art agentic RL systems: (1) Slime ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) is one of the most widely used open-source frameworks for agentic RL training. It adopts trajectory-level scheduling and may suffer from turn-level agentic bubbles. (2) RollFlash ( Lu et al., 2025b ) disaggregates environment controller from rollout controller, adopting action-level scheduling policy. It allows one sample’s tool execution to overlap with the another sample’s generation, thereby improving GPU utilization. (3) ThunderAgent ( Kang et al., 2026 ) abstracts agentic workflows as programs and adopts a program-aware scheduler that mitigates KV Cache thrashing by proactively evicting shorter contexts under memory pressure. Notably, given that the SWE-agent workload produces extremely long responses under our setting, we enable the hierarchical cache (HiCache) in SGLang ( contributors, 2025 ) to support offloading KV Cache to L2 host memory. To ensure fair comparison, we bump the sglang version to 0.5.17 and keep all the framework or algorithm arguments consistent. 6.2. End-to-End Performance Training performance. We first benchmark VenusRL against three state-of-the-art agentic RL systems on training performance across different settings. The async_factor set here controls the maximum staleness samples allowed in each rollout step. In particular, setting async_factor to 1.0 effectively enforces strict on-policy RL training. Figure 11 . Reward score for training. Figure 12 . Weight version heatmap comparison. 1) End-to-End Training Speed. Figure 10 presents the end-to-end training throughput across various batch sizes and async_factor configurations. Across both models, VenusRL consistently outperforms all three baselines across all settings, achieving 1.07–3.26 × \times speedup over Slime, 1.06-4.24 × \times speedup over RollFlash, and 1.05–2.67 × \times speedup over ThunderAgent. Even under strict on-policy training, i.e., async_factor =1.0, VenusRL improves throughput in every setting: by 1.07–1.15 × \times for Qwen3-4B and 1.05–1.85 × \times for Qwen3-32B. This gain mainly comes from the priority-aware KV Cache residency, which prioritizes evicting unused KV pages before evicting prefix pages referenced by in-flight trajectories. In addition, runtime request orchestration balances the sample distribution across rollout workers, further explaining the gain. When async_factor increases to 1.5 or 2.0, the speedup at batch size 16 remains modest at 1.06–1.17 × \times , consistent with limited KV cache contention and fewer opportunities for priority-aware scheduling. At batch sizes 32 and 64, VenusRL achieves 1.26–1.71 × \times speedup for Qwen3-4B and 1.64–4.24 × \times for Qwen3-32B. The experimental results demonstrate the strong scalability of VenusRL for agentic RL training. 2) Convergence and Stability. Figure 11 presents the reward score of Slime, Rollflash and VenusRL under 1.5 async_factor and 32 batch size setting. All three systems converge to nearly identical rewards within comparable steps. We observe similar convergence behavior across all evaluated settings; due to space limitations, we only report this representative setting. Figure 12 shows weight-version heatmaps across trajectory length percentiles, accumulated over 100 training steps with Qwen3-4B. VenusRL incurs no higher long-tail discard rate than Slime or Rollflash, justifying our design choice. Notably, we observe higher long-tail discard rate in Rollflash, which stems from action-level scheduling. Without special handling, stale trajectories repeatedly compete with newer samples and their progresses are continuously blocked. Figure 13 . Online sandbox Memory occupancy. Figure 14 . Throughput under limited resources. Environment management. As discussed in § 2 , memory capacity is the primary bottleneck that caps sandbox deployment density. Figure 14 thus profiles node memory occupancy over a three-hour online run case on a 400GB node. Native E2B admits sandboxes by configured peak memory. Occupancy saturates at about 8 % 8\% and stays flat for the rest of the run, leaving over 90 % 90\% of node memory unusable. In contrast, VenusRL admits sandbox based on actual memory usage and keeps occupancy in a high band between roughly 80% and 95%. At minute 132, a burst-growth of sandbox footprint drives the node occupancy to the capacity line within a single control interval. Rather than surrendering the node to the kernel OOM killer, VenusRL triggers targeted sandbox migration and returns occupancy in under 3 seconds (§ 6.4 ). In production, such issue is near zero with a well-tuned admission-threshold (specified in Appendix D ). We deliberately select a window that contains one such event to show how VenusRL behaves under residual OOM pressure. Figure 14 evaluates how environment concurrency backpressures rollout efficiency when sandbox resources are constrained, with 32 batch size and 1.5 async_factor setting. As is depicted, throughput drops to 0.81 × \times at 320 concurrent sandboxes and to 0.51 × \times at 256, respectively. The data indicates that without high-density sandbox deployment, the limited sandbox resources may directly degrade training performance and hide the efficiency of priority-aware scheduler. 6.3.
